DisneyANAHEIM, Calif. — A robot of Olaf, the beloved character from Walt Disney's hit animated film "Frozen," greeted Disney fans on the 15th local time, as the company moves to expand its deployment of AI-powered characters across its theme parks.Olaf was introduced at a Walt Disney Imagineering (WDI) pavilion exhibit during the D23 event at the Anaheim Convention Center in California. WDI is the organization that develops new spaces and content for Disney's theme parks, resorts and cruise businesses. D23 opened the previous day.Disney developed the Olaf robot with Nvidia, a maker of AI chips, and Google DeepMind, a developer of AI models. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang unveiled the Olaf robot at GTC 2026, a technology conference, this past March, and the robot was put into service late that month when the Frozen-themed world opened at Disney Adventure World in Paris. Olaf runs on Nvidia's AI chip software, including CUDA and Isaac.David Lightbody (second from left), senior vice president of Disney Live Entertainment; Kyle Laughlin, senior vice president of research and development; and Zack Riddley, senior vice president of global creative strategy, take part in a panel discussion for the media on Nov. 13 (local time). DisneyKey planners at Disney's theme parks said AI is playing a major role in bringing characters to life and that advances in AI will soon turn characters from its content into robots deployed throughout its parks. Disney held a media briefing with Imagineering executives on the 13th local time. Those attending included David Lightbody, senior vice president of live entertainment; Kyle Laughlin, senior vice president of research and development; and Zach Riddley, senior vice president of global creative strategy.Imagineering, a term combining "imagine" and "engineering," is the core organization that plans, designs and develops Disney's theme parks. It employs a diverse group of experts across more than 100 fields, including artists, architects, scientists, producers, programmers, builders and mathematicians. It brings Disney's signature characters to life at its parks and resorts and gives visitors distinctive experiences.The roughly 90-centimeter Olaf has been a talking point among visitors since it was deployed in late March. One moment, in which Olaf tripped while roaming the park and lost its carrot nose, drew attention online. Disney plans to expand deployment of AI robots like Olaf to its theme parks and cruises as part of its live entertainment."Developing Lucky the dinosaur in the past took years, but thanks to AI technology we built Olaf in four months," Laughlin said. "We have an incredible platform capable of bringing countless robots to life." He stressed: "In the not-too-distant future, we can imagine a world where freely roaming robots serve as tools for live entertainment, helping audiences experience things directly. We can actually build what you imagine. We will absolutely make it happen."A robot of Olaf, the character from Frozen, appears on stage at the Anaheim Convention Center in California on Nov. 15 (local time).
